You're right, and it isn't pedantry. The p-value is P(data this extreme or more | H0 true). A "97% chance the hypothesis is true" is P(hypothesis | data), a different quantity that also requires a prior. Equating them is the transposed-conditional fallacy.

The gap is large in practice. Under the Sellke-Bayarri-Berger calibration, p = 0.03 corresponds to a Bayes factor against H0 of at most about 3.5 (1/(−e·p·ln p)). With a 50/50 prior, that gives P(H1 | data) ≈ 78% at best, not 97%. With a more skeptical prior of 10% for H1, it drops to about 28%. The less plausible the hypothesis was beforehand, the further the true probability falls below 97%.

Your colleague's heuristic only holds when the prior is very favorable, and in that case it's an assumption, not something the p-value tells you.
